name: Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection
title: Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection
answer: Testing a study design before data collection is the practice of using simulation, power analysis, and protocol review to check whether a planned quantitative study can answer its research question. It covers the choice of estimand, sample size, measurement strategy, and analysis plan before any real participant or observational data are gathered. The goal is to catch design flaws, unrealistic assumptions, and underpowered comparisons while changes are still cheap. In reproducible quantitative work this stage also produces a written analysis plan that can be registered or shared.

sections.body: Testing a study design before data collection is the practice of using simulation, power analysis, and protocol review to check whether a planned quantitative study can answer its research question. It covers the choice of estimand, sample size, measurement strategy, and analysis plan before any real participant or observational data are gathered. The goal is to catch design flaws, unrealistic assumptions, and underpowered comparisons while changes are still cheap. In reproducible quantitative work this stage also produces a written analysis plan that can be registered or shared.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work usually runs on standard statistical computing environments such as R or Python, with simulation code kept in version control. A design test may use a few hundred lines of script to generate synthetic datasets, fit the planned model, and summarise performance across many repetitions. Cloud or local compute is enough for most power simulations, though larger factorial designs can require parallel execution. Reproducibility depends on recording the software versions, random seeds, and package dependencies used for each simulation run.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical workflow starts by writing down the target estimand and the exact analysis model that will be applied to the real data. The researcher then specifies a data generating process, including plausible effect sizes, noise, missingness, and any clustering or confounding. Simulated datasets are drawn many times under both null and alternative conditions, and the planned analysis is run on each draw to estimate power, bias, coverage, and false positive rates. The design is adjusted, for example by increasing sample size or changing the measurement schedule, and the simulation is repeated until the operating characteristics are acceptable. The final analysis plan and simulation code are then frozen before real data collection begins.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk concerns at this stage are mostly about transparency and provenance rather than participant data, because no real observations have been collected. Pre-registration of the design and analysis plan reduces the risk of later selective reporting or p-hacking. When synthetic data are generated from a real pilot dataset, the researcher must still respect the original consent and privacy conditions. Simulation code, seeds, and version history should be preserved so that an independent reviewer can reproduce the design checks and trace why a given sample size or model was chosen.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The practice is moving toward more automated design checking, where a proposed analysis plan is run against a battery of simulated scenarios before any data collection is approved. Generative models are increasingly used to create realistic synthetic datasets that preserve the correlation structure of a target population without exposing real records. Registered reports and journal workflows are making pre-data design tests a visible part of the publication record. Over time, design simulation may become a standard continuous step in research pipelines, with updated power and bias checks whenever the protocol or model changes.
